Spot fake apps and malicious QR codes before acting on them
Reduce the information that oversharing and accidental leaks hand to others

lessons.title: Social engineering and the new face of impersonation

blocks.text: **Social engineering** means manipulating a person, rather than breaking software, to get what the attacker wants. The target is trust. Everything in Module 4 is a form of it, and the pattern shows up in many other places too.
Almost every social engineering attempt uses the same handful of levers. Knowing them is a better defence than memorising any single scam.

blocks.caption: The levers of social engineering
headers: What the attacker says or does
rows: Pretends to be a boss, bank, police officer or support technician
Ask who they are, then call back on an official number
'This must happen in the next ten minutes'
Slow down; real obligations survive a short check
Uses a friend's name, a colleague's name or details from your social media
Remember that details can be collected; verify the request itself
Asks for a small favour, such as forwarding a code
Notice when the favour involves access or money
Threatens a penalty, or promises a prize or refund
Treat strong emotion as a reason to pause

blocks.text: Cloned voices and fake video

Artificial intelligence now makes it possible to copy a person's voice from a short clip, and to create convincing fake video. Scammers have started to use these tools. The result might be a phone call from what sounds like your daughter, in tears, asking for urgent money. Or a video call in which a senior person seems to ask a finance clerk to make a payment.

This is a new costume on an old plot. The person is not who they appear to be, and the call pushes you to act fast and in secret. You cannot reliably tell a good fake from a real voice by listening, so do not rely on your ears. Rely on the process.

blocks.title: A family safe word
blocks.text: Agree on a private word or question with close family, something that is not on social media. If an urgent call asks for money, ask for it. Real relatives will understand; a cloned voice cannot know it.

blocks.title: The director on video
blocks.text: A finance assistant is invited to a short video call where the managing director asks for an urgent payment to a new supplier. The face and voice seem right. Company policy says any new bank detail must be confirmed by a call to a known number, so she ends the call and phones the director's usual cellphone. He knows nothing about it. The rule saved the company, not her ability to spot a fake.

For workplaces and small businesses, a simple rule does the work: **no payment, bank detail change or sensitive information is released on the strength of a single call, message or video.** Confirm through a second channel, and require a second person for large payments if you have one.

blocks.prompt: What is the most reliable protection against a cloned voice asking you for urgent money?
options: Listening carefully for robotic sounds
Agreeing a verification routine, such as a family safe word and a call-back on a known number
Answering questions quickly before you get confused
Asking the caller to repeat themselves
blocks.explain: You cannot count on spotting a fake by ear. A prepared verification routine works regardless of how convincing the voice is.

lessons.title: Credential stuffing, fake apps and malicious QR codes

blocks.text: This lesson covers three threats that look different but share a theme: they work because of ordinary habits. Understanding how they work shows you what to change.
Credential stuffing

When a website is breached, lists of email addresses and passwords end up in criminals' hands. **Credential stuffing** is when software automatically tries those pairs on other popular services, such as email, online shops and streaming. It is not clever and it is not personal. It is a numbers game that costs the attacker almost nothing.

It only works on people who **reuse passwords**. If your leaked forum password is not used anywhere else, the attempt fails. This is the plainest argument for a unique password on every account, and for turning on multi-factor authentication, which stops a correct password from being enough by itself.

blocks.title: The streaming surprise
blocks.text: Amahle gets an email that a login occurred from another country on her streaming account. She did not do it, but years ago she used the same password on a small shopping site that was later breached. She changes the password, switches on a second sign-in step, and then updates the same password on two other accounts she had forgotten about.
Fake apps

Criminals publish apps that imitate banks, delivery services, popular games or well-known tools. Some sit in official stores for a while before being removed, and others are offered as direct downloads through links in messages. They may ask for your login, or request permissions that let them read messages and watch what you do.

items: Go to your bank's or service's official website and follow its link to the right app, instead of searching the store by name.
Check the developer name, the number of downloads and the recent reviews, and be wary of an app with a brand-new account behind it.
Never install an app from a link sent in a message, or by switching on installs from unknown sources.
Notice odd permission requests, such as a calculator wanting to read your texts.

blocks.text: Malicious QR codes

A **QR code** is just a picture that holds a web address or other text. It is not dangerous in itself, but you cannot read where it leads. Criminals stick their own code over a genuine one on a parking meter or poster, or send one in an email, hoping you will scan without thinking, which is the QR version of phishing.

blocks.title: Scan with care
blocks.text: After scanning, read the address your phone shows before you open it. If a code leads you to log in or pay, ask whether you expected that. If a sticker looks pasted over another one, do not use it. Type the official address instead.

blocks.prompt: Why does credential stuffing fail against a person who uses a different password on every site?
options: Leaked passwords stop working after a month
A password leaked from one site does not unlock the other accounts
Websites block all automated login attempts
Criminals do not collect passwords from breaches
blocks.explain: Credential stuffing relies on reuse. A unique password means a leak at one service reveals nothing that works elsewhere.

blocks.prompt: A QR code on a poster or parking meter is safe as long as it is printed professionally.
options: True
False
blocks.explain: Criminals can paste their own code over a real one. Always check where the code leads before entering any details.

lessons.title: Oversharing, accidental leaks and a threat spotter's checklist

blocks.text: Not every leak is stolen. A great deal of information escapes because we hand it out ourselves, in small harmless-looking pieces. Social engineers are happy to collect them, because each piece makes the next lie more convincing.

Think about what a stranger could learn from your public posts: your full name, workplace, school, pets' names, your birthday, holiday dates, your home from the background of a photo. Several of those are also the answers to common security questions, and some appear in people's passwords.

blocks.title: The holiday post
blocks.text: Zodwa posts photos from her beach holiday with the caption 'Back on the 28th!' and a tag of her home suburb. She has just told the world her house will be empty, and given a convincing detail for a caller who rings her mother pretending to be her.
Habits that cut the leak

items: Review privacy settings on each social account, and limit who sees your posts and friends list.
Post holiday photos after you return rather than during the trip.
Check the background of photos for house numbers, ID documents, boarding passes, screens and street signs.
Do not post photos of tickets, cards or documents, even partly covered. Barcodes and numbers can still be read.
Use answers to security questions that are not true, and store them in your password manager.

blocks.text: Accidental leaks

A surprising number of leaks are plain mistakes. An email goes to the wrong recipient. A shared folder is left open to anyone with the link. A spreadsheet with hidden columns still holds private data. A photo of a screen shows a password. A conversation in a group chat includes someone who should not be there.
The defence is slowing down at the moment of sending. Check the recipient, check what is attached, and check what access a link gives.

blocks.caption: Threat spotter's quick checklist
rows: Did this message or call arrive unexpectedly?
Do not act on it yet
Is it asking for money, a code, a login or secrecy?
Verify using a channel you choose
Treat the pressure as a warning
Did I find the app, link or code myself, or did someone hand it to me?
Go to the official source directly
Would I be comfortable if this post or file were public?
If not, do not share it that way

blocks.title: Your public footprint
blocks.intro: See yourself the way a stranger or a scammer would. Do this with your own accounts only.
tasks: Search for your own name in a search engine, and in the search or profile pages of your main social platforms while logged out. Note everything personal that appears.
Open your social media privacy settings. Tighten who can see your posts, friends list, phone number and birthday.
Scroll through your last twenty posts and mark any that reveal your home, routine, workplace, children or documents. Delete or edit those.
List your security-question answers on important accounts. If any can be found online, change them to something untrue and store them in your password manager.
Pick one family member and agree a verification routine, such as a safe word for urgent money requests.
blocks.reflection: What was the most surprising thing a stranger could learn about you in ten minutes?

blocks.prompt: You are about to share a shared-drive link to a spreadsheet of client details with one colleague. Which approach best avoids an accidental leak?
options: Set it to anyone with the link and paste it in a large group chat
Share it with that colleague's named account only, and check the access setting
Send it as an attachment to several people in case they need it
Rename the file so it does not look sensitive
blocks.explain: Restricting access to named people and checking the setting limits who can open it. Open links and extra copies multiply the chance of leaks.

modules.title: Conducting a Personal Security Assessment
modules.summary: Bring the course together: inventory what you have, rate the risks, work through a checklist, follow a 30-day plan and know what to do after an incident.
objectives: Build an inventory of your accounts, devices and important information
Rate risks using likelihood and impact, and choose what to fix first
Complete a security checklist and a prioritised 30-day action plan
Respond calmly and in the right order after a security incident

lessons.title: Inventory first, then rate the risks

blocks.text: A security assessment sounds formal. For a person or a small business it is simply an honest look at what you have, what could go wrong and what to do about it first. Professionals use the same three steps on much larger organisations.
You cannot protect what you have forgotten about. So begin with a list.
Step one: the inventory

Write down your **accounts**, your **devices** and your **important information**. Do not aim for perfection. Aim for the ones that would hurt if they were lost or taken over. A password manager's list, your phone's installed apps and your email's old receipts are good places to jog your memory.
Notice how a table like this already shows the gaps. Two rows are the obvious worry, and you did not need any technical knowledge to see it.
Step two: rate the risk

**Risk** is a mix of two things: how **likely** a bad event is, and how bad the **impact** would be. For each item, give likelihood and impact a simple score of low, medium or high. You are not calculating anything exact. You are deciding where to look first.

blocks.caption: Likelihood and impact, simply
rows: Plan for it, for example with a backup

blocks.title: Rating Thandi's list
blocks.text: Her customer spreadsheet is on an unlocked laptop with no backup. A stolen bag or a dead hard drive is quite likely, and losing the order book would be serious. High likelihood, high impact: fix first. Her old streaming login is reused but holds little of value. Fix when convenient.

blocks.title: Impact is about what it connects to
blocks.text: As Module 1 showed, an account's impact depends on what it can unlock. Your email and your phone number almost always rate high, even if they hold nothing exciting.

blocks.prompt: In a simple risk rating, which item should you fix first?
options: Low likelihood and low impact
High likelihood and high impact
High likelihood and low impact
Low likelihood and medium impact
blocks.explain: Risk combines how likely something is with how much it would hurt. High on both means it goes to the top of your list.

lessons.title: The checklist and your 30-day plan

blocks.text: With your inventory and risk ratings in hand, you need a plan you can actually follow. A long to-do list that nobody finishes protects nobody. A short list in the right order does.
The checklist below pulls together the biggest wins from the course. Tick what you already do, and the unticked items become your plan.

blocks.label: Personal security checklist
blocks.text:
ACCOUNTS
[ ] Main email has a long unique password and the strongest second factor on offer
[ ] Banking, cloud storage and password manager have a second factor
[ ] I use a password manager and no password is reused
[ ] Recovery codes are stored in my password manager or printed somewhere safe
[ ] WhatsApp two-step verification is on

DEVICES
[ ] Phone and laptop have screen locks and encryption on
[ ] Automatic updates are on for the system, browser and apps
[ ] Find-my-device is switched on and tested
[ ] Router admin password changed and firmware updated

DATA
[ ] Important files follow 3-2-1 and a restore has been tested
[ ] I have deleted old sensitive files and unused accounts

HABITS
[ ] I verify money, code and login requests through a second channel
[ ] I only install from official stores and maker websites
[ ] Social media privacy settings are reviewed
[ ] My family has a verification routine for urgent requests
Putting it in order
Order matters because some steps protect everything else. If your email is weak, every other improvement leans on a cracked foundation. So start there.

blocks.caption: A suggested 30-day plan
rows: Email password and second factor, password manager set up with a strong master passphrase, recovery codes saved
Bank and payment apps, cloud storage and WhatsApp second factor; replace reused passwords on your five most important accounts
Updates, screen locks, encryption, find-my-device, router settings, a backup and one test restore
Social media settings, deleting old data and accounts, family verification routine, a calendar reminder to repeat this review

blocks.title: Small and finishable beats big and abandoned
blocks.text: Aim for about thirty to sixty minutes a few times a week. If a week slips, carry the tasks forward. A plan that bends is better than one that breaks.

blocks.title: Sipho's plan
blocks.text: Sipho's inventory shows his email has no second factor and his forum password is reused on his email. In week one he changes the email password, adds an authenticator app and prints recovery codes. By week four he has fixed his five main accounts, backed up his photos and set a diary reminder for six months ahead.

blocks.title: Run your own security assessment
blocks.intro: This is the capstone exercise. Set aside about an hour for the first pass, and use your own accounts and devices only.
tasks: Build your inventory: list at least ten accounts, your devices, and the important information you hold. Use a table like the one in the previous lesson.
Rate each item for likelihood and impact, and mark the ones that fall in the top-priority boxes.
Work through the personal security checklist and tick only what is true today.
Turn the unticked items into a dated 30-day plan, with no more than four or five tasks per week and the email account first.
Complete the first task from week one before you stop.
blocks.reflection: Which three items would make the biggest difference if you did only them?

blocks.prompt: Why does a 30-day security plan usually start with your main email account?
options: Email is the most fun account to secure
A weak email account can be used to reset many other accounts
Email is the only account that needs a password
Email providers insist on it
blocks.explain: Password resets usually go to your email, so protecting it first stops weak spots elsewhere from being used against you.

lessons.title: When something goes wrong: incident response and keeping it up

blocks.text: However careful you are, one day something may slip through. A phishing page fools you, a device is stolen, a service you use is breached. What you do in the first hour matters more than how embarrassed you feel.
Plan for it now, when you are calm. Think of it like knowing where the fire extinguisher is.

blocks.title: The first response to any incident

items.title: Stop and contain
items.text: Disconnect an affected device from the internet, close the suspicious page, and stop responding to the person contacting you.

items.title: Secure your email and key accounts
items.text: From a clean device, change passwords for your email first, then banking and other important accounts, and check for sign-ins you do not recognise.

items.title: Call the people who can act
items.text: Phone your bank on the number on your card if money or card details are involved, and your mobile provider if your number may have been taken over.

items.title: Preserve evidence
items.text: Keep messages, screenshots, emails and transaction details. They help banks, employers and the police.

items.title: Report and warn
items.text: Report the scam to the organisation being imitated and to the relevant authority, and warn people who might receive follow-up messages from your accounts.

items.title: Review and improve
items.text: Once things are calm, ask what let it happen and which layer would have stopped it, then add that layer.

blocks.text: Different incidents need different emphasis. The table gives a quick guide, and the general steps above apply in every case.

blocks.caption: Quick guide by incident
rows: Clicked a phishing link and typed a password
Change that password and any reused ones
Turn on a second factor and check recent activity
Watch statements and expect follow-up scams
Lock or locate it, and block the SIM
Secure email, then restore second factors
Get help, then restore from backup
Recover through the official process and change the password
Tell your contacts not to trust messages from that account

blocks.title: Speed beats shame
blocks.text: People who report quickly lose less. Banks and providers see these cases every day. They are much more interested in stopping the damage than in judging you.
Keeping it up

Security is a habit, not a project. Set a reminder for every six months to repeat a short version of the assessment: new accounts, retired devices, a test restore, a look at what has changed in your life. People change jobs, buy phones and start businesses, and each one changes what needs protecting.

blocks.title: Write your incident card
blocks.intro: Prepare now so you are not working it out in a panic. Keep the finished card somewhere safe that does not depend on your phone.
tasks: Write the contact numbers for your bank, card issuer and mobile provider, copied from your card or the official website rather than a message.
Note where your recovery codes, backup drive and a second trusted device are.
Write the first three actions you will take if your phone is lost, if you click a phishing link and if your laptop is locked by a ransom note.
Share the card's location, not its contents, with one trusted person.
blocks.reflection: Which of your accounts would be hardest to recover, and what could you do this week to make that easier?

blocks.prompt: You gave your card details to a convincing caller a minute ago. What is the most urgent step?
options: Wait to see if any charge appears
Phone your bank on the number on your card and report it
Post a warning on social media first
Change your Wi-Fi password
blocks.explain: Your bank can block the card and stop fraudulent payments quickly. Speed limits the loss.

blocks.prompt: Select all the steps that belong in a first response to a suspected account takeover.
options: Secure your email and key accounts from a clean device
Preserve messages and screenshots as evidence
Delete every record so nothing can be found
Warn contacts not to trust messages from that account
blocks.explain: Securing accounts, keeping evidence and warning contacts all limit harm. Deleting records removes information that helps investigators and your bank.
